President Roosevelt sent a message to Secretary of State Cordell Hull on December 23, 1943, two days before Christmas and a fortnight after his return from Tehran and Cairo. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

The weeks after a summit are when its promises meet the machinery of government. Roosevelt's messages to Hull in this period passed decisions and problems from the traveling President to the department that had to execute them. For readers, this cable belongs to the unglamorous but decisive phase of diplomacy: turning handshakes in Tehran into instructions, appointments, and orders in Washington.
frus-1944-quebec-d28:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 23, 1944, the day Paris rose against its occupiers. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

The last week of August 1944 carried the alliance from campaigning to conferring: France was being liberated, and the Quebec meeting was three weeks off. Roosevelt's correspondence then had to ready the big unsettled questions, above all Germany's treatment and the terms of continued aid to Britain. For readers, this message stands at the turn of the season, written while the guns were still firing in Paris.
frus-1944-quebec-d128:
From Moscow on September 10, 1944, Ambassador Harriman urgently summarized for Roosevelt and Hull the Soviet reply on Warsaw aid. The British ambassador had shown him the message Moscow sent London. Harriman called it an extremely shrewd statement for the record, one that shifted the decision, and the blame, onto the Western allies.

In paraphrase, Moscow said real aid would come from the Red Army's advance. Supply drops, it claimed, had repeatedly fallen into German hands. Still, the Soviets were prepared to join a drop operation under a prearranged plan. Harriman asked for urgent instructions on whether to open talks with the Red Army staff, and noted he lacked fresh word on how much of Warsaw the insurgents still held.
frus-1944-quebec-d228:
Hull cabled Harriman on September 12, 1944, with the president's instructions on Warsaw. Marshall was being directed to have General Deane explore the Soviet offer to cooperate in aid, working with his British colleagues. Harriman was to lend Deane every support and tell Molotov that America was prepared to do its utmost, jointly with the British and Russians, on immediate aid to the garrison.

Hull added a political warning. The Soviet decision might come too late if the garrison had shrunk too far for drops to be practical, but that question would emerge in negotiation. What mattered was that Washington show no hesitation in implementing the Soviet promise, so it could not be blamed if aid failed to arrive in time.

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d128:
One flaw in the Germany plan bothered the President: no tough civilian voice in Berlin. Leo Pasvolsky recorded the objection on 15 November 1944, after a White House talk on the treatment of Germany. His memorandum is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Roosevelt had read the State Department's memorandum and found it satisfactory except on this point. As he saw it, Eisenhower and the British and Russian commanders would run their zones. A commission of lower-ranking soldiers would sit in Berlin. What it lacked was a strong civilian point of view. His fix: give a general's commission to some outstanding civilian and make him the American member of the Berlin commission.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d228:
Leave the Turkish Straits alone: that is the hope stated in a briefing paper of 21 October 1944. The “Memorandum Regarding the Question of the Turkish Straits” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It gives three reasons for wishing the subject never came up.

First, the Montreux Convention of 1936 has worked well, and Moscow itself said so, jointly with Britain, in 1941. The Straits went unused as a supply road to Russia because the Axis held the lands around them, not because of the treaty. Second, large changes would likely violate Turkish sovereignty and upset the balance in the Balkans and the Near East. Turkey, the paper adds, has been a good custodian of the Straits. Minor changes from Moscow or London would still be weighed with care.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d328:

Stalin agreed, reporting that Soviet armies were moving with success toward the line of the Oder.

Yield like water, desire little, and let people and events follow their own course: that counsel repeats in cryptic, compressed lines. Chinese thought on power and humility has drawn on these chapters for two millennia. English readers of Legge's version meet the text in formal Victorian dress, which can feel distant, yet the paradoxes still cut against ambition and control.
tob-10628:
Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri, a blind Syrian poet who died over a thousand years ago, filled his Diwan with rhymed meditations on fate and folly. He was a skeptic in a religious age. His verses distrust clerics, pity the credulous, and urge doing no harm to any living thing; he himself lived as a strict vegetarian.

Poems in the collection turn over death, hypocrisy, ambition, and the vanity of sects that kill over doctrine. The voice is bleak and brilliant at once, funny in its contempt and tender toward animals and outcasts. English readers meet a freethinker from the medieval Arab world who sounds startlingly modern.
tob-10828:
Annie Besant edited the posthumous third volume of The Secret Doctrine from H. P. Blavatsky's remaining papers. Its subjects shift from cosmic theory toward occult practice and esoteric history. Because Blavatsky did not live to shape it, the volume is more fragmentary than the first two books of the set.

Loose papers on hidden teachings, initiates, and disputed points of doctrine read like notes from a workshop rather than a finished system. Scholars debate how much reflects Blavatsky's final intentions. V1 evidence directs the volume to committed students of Theosophy rather than beginners; newcomers should start with her Key to Theosophy and return here for depth.
tob-4028:
Immanuel Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, asking what reason can and cannot know. His answer reshaped philosophy: we know things as they appear to us, never things in themselves, because space, time, and causality are forms our own mind imposes on experience. Kant called the shift his Copernican revolution in thought.

God, freedom, and immortality fall outside theoretical proof, though they return as needs of moral life. The prose is formidable, architected like a cathedral, and readers should expect slow going. Two centuries of argument later, the Critique remains the mountain modern philosophy is still climbing or deliberately circling.

Augustine of Hippo wrote The City of God across the years after Rome's sack in 410, and Marcus Dods's translation presents volume one here. Pagans charged that Christians had caused the disaster by abandoning the old gods. Augustine answers that Rome's gods failed long before Christ, and that Rome's own vices, celebrated by its historians, rotted it from within.

From that defense grows his larger vision of two cities, earthly and divine, contending through history toward judgment. The first volume handles Rome's religion and early calamities in detail. Few books have taught the West to think historically as this one did; volume one lays the foundation stone by stone.
tob-4128:
Mead's 1896 Pistis Sophia, translated from the Coptic, gave modern readers their first full Gnostic gospel. The risen Savior teaches his disciples for years after the resurrection, the text claims, and at its heart stands Pistis Sophia, Faith-Wisdom, a fallen power who repents through the aeons.

Her thirteen repentances, sung as psalms, plead for rescue from the rulers of darkness. Jesus answers with readings of psalms and odes as coded accounts of her fall. The cosmology is vast and strange. Verified from the 1919 edition, Mead's version introduced Gnosticism to the modern world and still opens the subject.
tob-13328:
Valmiki, the sage poet of ancient India, composed the Ramayana, one of the two great Sanskrit epics. R. T. H. Griffith turned it into English verse in the nineteenth century. The epic holds a central place in Hindu life and art across Asia.

Prince Rama is exiled to the forest with his wife Sita and his brother Lakshmana. When the demon king Ravana steals Sita away to Lanka, Rama allies with the monkey host and wages war to win her back. The seven books join high adventure to dharma, the law of duty that Rama's life displays in full.
podcast-tuckercarlson-qk3I6xi7c28:
Tucker Carlson sits with Donald Trump and asks him flat out what truly happened to Jeffrey Epstein. The episode title is built on that one exchange. Carlson puts the question that hangs over the whole case.

Trump gives his answer on the death and the files in his own words. Carlson presses on what the public still does not know. The clip of the clash is the heart of the episode. Listeners can hear the exchange whole, not cut into bits by the press. The library keeps the talk as a record of that rare, blunt moment.
podcast-joerogan-7-IOCUCDL28:
Episode 377 of the Joe Rogan Experience catches Duncan Trussell in the show's early, wild years. Trussell, a comedian with a mystic streak, was already a core member of Rogan's circle. The young show had fewer rules then, and this visit shows it.

The talk jumps between psychedelic stories, jokes about the self, and sudden deep turns on love and death. Trussell's free, riffing style fills the room, and Rogan matches his energy. Listeners who know Trussell's later, calmer work will hear the rawer version here, a snapshot of podcasting before the format grew polished.
corti-reign-of-the-house-of-rothschild-1:
Egon Caesar Corti, an Austrian historian, wrote The Reign of the House of Rothschild from the family's own papers. The English edition came out at New York in 1928. It covers the banking house from 1830 to 1871, its years of greatest power in Europe.

Corti follows the five Rothschild houses as they lend to kings, fund railways, and move money across borders. Letters and deals show how the family turned credit into sway over states. The book stays a rich source on the age when private bankers stood beside thrones. His access to the family archives gave the book its lasting weight.
keightley-fairy-mythology-1828:
Thomas Keightley, an Irish writer and scholar, published The Fairy Mythology in 1828. The text here follows the enlarged edition of 1892. Keightley ranged across Europe comparing the fairy beliefs of many peoples, the first broad survey of its kind.

He sorts elves, dwarfs, trolls, and household spirits by country and by kind. Tales from Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia, and beyond sit side by side so their kinship shows. He also covers mermaids and other beings of the sea. The book helped found the study of folklore, and its tales still charm readers.
osborn-man-rises-to-parnassus-1928:
Henry Fairfield Osborn delivered these Princeton lectures in 1928 under the title Man Rises to Parnassus. The museum leader used them to state his mature view of human prehistory. He organized the past around what he called critical epochs.

Osborn promoted a dawn-man theory and looked to central Asia for human origins. Both ideas won influence in his lifetime and were later abandoned. The lectures show his gift for grand, readable synthesis. They also preserve the last strong statement of views that new fossils soon displaced. The lectures were printed for a general audience, not only for specialists.
fortune-esoteric-orders-and-their-work-1:
How the mystery schools truly work was Dion Fortune's subject in 1928. The Esoteric Orders and Their Work surveys the Western orders from inside knowledge. Fortune wrote as one who had trained in them and led her own school.

She sets out their grades, their methods of work, and the ends they claim to serve. The book sorts true training from sham and tells the seeker what to expect at each step of the road. Few English books of its time spoke so plainly on the subject. It opened the doors of the orders to the plain reader.
champollion-precis-lettre-dacier-1828:
Jean-Francois Champollion taught the world to read Egypt's script in his Precis of 1828, with his famed note of 1822 bound in. Champollion had cracked the script by the stone of Rosetta and years of keen work. Here he sets out the whole scheme: which signs stand for sounds, which for things, and how scribes mixed them.

The book, in French, is the birth note of a whole field. Each claim rests on texts fans can check. Champollion died young, ere he saw Egypt in full. This work is the key that still unlocks its tombs.
champollion-lettres-egypte-nubie-1828:
Jean-Francois Champollion wrote home from his great trek in Letters from Egypt and Nubia, writ in 1828 and 1829. At last the man who cracked the script stood ere the tombs he had read on paper. He sails the Nile, reads walls at sight, and writes with joy, heat, and awe in each note home.

He sorts kings, dates, and gods as he goes, oft righting old claims. The notes were set in print for the crowd in France. They read as a log of a mind at its peak. The field's first field notes still charm.
spence-mysteries-britain-1928:
Lewis Spence, a Scots writer on myth and folk lore, wrote this survey of the hidden rites of Britain in 1928. He had spent years on the myths of many lands. Here he turned to the isle he knew best and its deep past.

Spence walked from the druids to the great stone rings and the lore of old shrines. He held that a native rite line ran through British life from the far past. Some claims go past the proof, but the book sums up his case in one place.
corti-rise-of-the-house-of-rothschild-19:
Egon Caesar Corti, an Austrian writer, made this full history of the rise of the Rothschild house in 1928. Brian and Beatrix Lunn turned it into English, and it came out in New York the same year. Corti worked from the family's own store of papers, a rare chance for a writer.

The book tells how Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt and his five sons built a bank that spanned Europe. Wars, state loans, and swift news fill the years from 1770 to 1830 in his tale. Later books on the house all cite Corti as their chief source.
dobie-tales-old-time-texas-1928:
J. Frank Dobie spent his life gathering the folk tales of Texas. His Tales of Old-Time Texas, from 1928, sets down tales heard from ranch hands and old-timers. Dobie wrote them in a warm, plain style. The book holds a firm place in Texas letters.

One tale stands out for fans of strange lore. The Wild Woman of the Navidad haunted river lands in the 1830s and later years. Dobie gives the hunts, tracks, and fears tied to her name. Other tales tell of lost gold, ghosts, and hard men. The set keeps a lost Texas alive.
summers-vampire-kith-kin-1928:
Montague Summers gave the vampire its first full study in 1928. The Vampire: His Kith and Kin draws on lore from all over the world. Summers was a priest who took the old tales in full earnest. He treats the vampire as a true foe of man and God.

Tales from Greece, Slav lands, and the far East fill the book. He sorts the kinds of the undead and tells how men fought them. Church law, trial tales, and folk rites all get a place. The book set the base for all grave study of the vampire since.
law-serious-call-1728:
William Law wrote A Serious Call to a Devout and Holy Life in 1728. Law was an English priest who gave up his post for his views. The book bids each Christian to live each day for God. It shaped John Wesley, George Whitefield, and the great church revolt of the age.

Law shows how prayer, work, food, and funds all fall under God's rule. He mocks half faith with tales of folk who pray well and live ill. His tone is strict, warm, and hard to shake off once read. The book stands as a peak of plain English works on the holy life.
hawthorne-fanshawe-1828:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Fanshawe in 1828, his first novel, issued anonymously at his own cost. He later tried to destroy every copy of the college romance he could find and burn. The book survives as the seed of the canon, essential to the origins of his art.

Fanshawe, a frail scholar at Harley College, wastes in study while a villain plots around him. Dr. Melmoth's ward Ellen is pursued by a scoundrel who lures her toward a cliff and death. Fanshawe saves her, renounces his hopeless love, and dies young of his scholar's ruined health in college. The plot is stock Gothic, but the gloom and guilt point straight to the later Hawthorne of Salem. He disowned the book so hard that his wife learned of it only late.
mckay-home-to-harlem-1928:
Claude McKay published Home to Harlem in 1928, his bestselling novel of Harlem nightlife and Black labor in prose. The landmark Harlem Renaissance novel follows Jake's return from war and wandering to the cabarets of Harlem in 1928. It was the first novel by a Black writer to reach the bestseller lists then.

Jake, a deserter from a labor battalion, comes home hungry for Harlem's music, food, and women of its nights. He loves Felice, loses her in a brawl, and searches the district's clubs and buffet flats for her. Ray, a Haitian waiter and writer, gives the pleasure chase a brooding, questioning second voice in the tale. McKay renders dialect, jazz, and street philosophy with a poet's ear and a radical's sympathy for workers. Du Bois scorned its cabaret focus, yet readers made it the Renaissance's popular breakthrough.
fauset-plum-bun-1928:
Jessie Redmon Fauset published Plum Bun in 1928, a novel about a young Black woman in Philadelphia and New York. Angela Murray is light-skinned and wants a career as an artist. She decides to pass as white to gain freedom and a chance at success. Her sister stays in the Black community they grew up in.

Angela finds that passing brings loneliness and fear of being found out. Love and ambition pull her in opposite ways. In time she questions the price of hiding who she is. The novel is praised for its clear-eyed view of race, gender, and the cost of ambition.
larsen-quicksand-1928:
Nella Larsen published Quicksand in 1928, her first novel. Helga Crane is a young woman of mixed Danish and Black heritage. She teaches at a Black school in the South and feels stifled there. She moves to Chicago, then Harlem, then Copenhagen, always hoping the next place will fit.

In Denmark she is prized as exotic yet still feels like an outsider. Back in Harlem, she seeks meaning and makes choices that trap her in a hard marriage in the South. Larsen writes with cool clarity about race, sex, and belonging. The novel is now a classic of the Harlem Renaissance.
yeats-tower-1928:
W. B. Yeats published The Tower in 1928, a book of poems written in his sixties. Yeats had bought and restored a Norman tower in Ireland as his home. Sailing to Byzantium opens the book with an old man's wish for a soul made like art. The title poem broods on age, memory, and imagination.

Meditations in Time of Civil War reflects on violence in Ireland after independence. Other poems address friends, ancestors, and the poet's own past loves. The style is grand, bitter, and full of strong images. Critics often call The Tower his finest single volume. It shows a great poet facing old age without flinching.
eddington-nature-physical-world-1928:
Arthur Eddington published The Nature of the Physical World in 1928, from his Gifford Lectures. Eddington was a leading astronomer who helped prove Einstein's theory. He explains relativity and quantum theory for general readers with rare skill. Physics, he argues, deals in symbols and pointer readings, not in the solid stuff of common sense.

His two tables, the familiar one and the scientific one, open the book famously. Later chapters turn to entropy, time's arrow, and the place of mind in nature. Eddington suggests the stuff of the world is mind-stuff at root. The book became a landmark of popular science. It shaped how a generation pictured physics.
freud-future-illusion-robson-scott-1928:
Sigmund Freud published The Future of an Illusion in German in 1927. The English text here is W. D. Robson-Scott's translation of 1928. Freud calls religion an illusion born of human wishes. Helpless before nature and fate, people create father-like gods for comfort and control. Civilization, he argues, rests in part on this shared wish.

He predicts that education and science will slowly loosen religion's hold. His dialogue partner raises objections, and Freud answers them in turn. The book is his clearest atheist manifesto. It angered believers and pleased free-thinkers in equal measure. Its debate on faith and reason continues today.
spengler-decline-west-vol-2-1928:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 2, appears in Atkinson's translation of 1928. Subtitled Perspectives of World-History, the volume completes Spengler's work. He turns to the state, money, and the destiny of peoples. Democracy, in his account, yields to money power and then to Caesarism, rule by strong men.

Spengler surveys cities, classes, and religions across his eight great cultures. The West's final phase, he predicts, will be an age of empire and engineering without new art. Many reject his fatalism; few ignore his sweep. The two volumes form a vast, gloomy system. They remain essential for the study of historical pessimism between the wars.
evans-wentz-milarepa-1928:
Walter Evans-Wentz, an American scholar of Celtic and Eastern religion, published Tibet's Great Yogi Milarepa in 1928. The book translates the beloved life of Milarepa, the eleventh-century Tibetan poet-saint who sang his teaching in verses. A Tibetan lama, Kazi Dawa-Samdup, did the base translation.

Milarepa's story runs from black magic and revenge in his youth to years of hard training under his teacher Marpa. His later life of caves, songs, and converts forms the heart of the book. The volume introduced Tibetan Buddhism's saints to the West in human, gripping form. Tibetan families still tell his story to children as a household tale.
raphael-manual-of-astrology-1828:
Raphael was the pen name of Robert Cross Smith, a London astrologer whose Manual of Astrology, or Book of the Stars, appeared in 1828. Astrology had sunk to almanac level in England, and Raphael set out to raise it. His manual became the founding text of the nineteenth-century astrological revival.

He teaches chart casting, nativities, and the judgment of daily questions in a brisk, popular style meant for self-taught readers. His almanacs and guides sold the art back to a Regency public that had nearly forgotten it. Every later English astrological writer worked in a market Raphael reopened.
nicholas-cusa-vision-of-god-salter-1928:
Emma Gurney Salter published her translation of Nicholas of Cusa's Vision of God in 1928, with an introduction by Evelyn Underhill. Cusa, a German cardinal and thinker, wrote De Visione Dei in 1453 for monks at Tegernsee. He sent them an icon of an all-seeing face with the book.

Cusa taught that God's gaze rests on each person wholly, and that opposites meet in God beyond reason's reach. His doctrine of learned ignorance held that knowing our ignorance is the start of wisdom. The short book blends prayer, logic, and mysticism. It bridges medieval devotion and Renaissance thought, and Salter's English made it a modern devotional classic.
epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-oldfath:
Volume 2 of Oldfather's Loeb Epictetus appeared in 1928, completing the set. It holds Books 3 and 4 of the Discourses as reported by Arrian, then the Enchiridion, or Manual, and the Fragments. An index closes the volume for study use.

The Enchiridion distills Epictetus's teaching into short rules for daily life: control what you can, accept what you cannot, and act with justice. Soldiers, monks, and prisoners have carried it for centuries. It is the most influential Stoic handbook ever written. With the Discourses complete beside it, Oldfather's second volume finishes the standard English Epictetus of the Loeb Classical Library.
galsworthy-swan-song-1928:
John Galsworthy closed the Forsyte chronicles with Swan Song, published in 1928. It ends both the second trilogy, A Modern Comedy, and Soames Forsyte's long story. Galsworthy had followed the family from Victorian wealth into the unsettled 1920s.

Fleur's unhappy love for Jon Forsyte burns on inside her marriage, while Soames grows old and oddly tender. The General Strike of 1926 shakes London in the background. A fire at Soames's house brings the saga's themes of property and love to a final test. Galsworthy gives his most possessive character a strangely moving end, and an age closes with him.
lawrence-lady-chatterley-1928:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Lady Chatterley's Lover in Italy and published it privately in Florence in 1928. No regular British or American publisher would touch it. Lawrence rewrote the novel three times before settling on this final version, the complete Florence text.

Connie Chatterley's husband Clifford returns from the war paralyzed and sealed into his mind. Connie slowly withers in their great house until she begins an affair with the gamekeeper, Mellors. Lawrence treats their love as a cure for a dead, mechanical age. The book was banned for obscenity for decades, then became a famous test case for free publication in 1960.
woolf-orlando-1928:
Virginia Woolf published Orlando in 1928 and called it a biography, though it breaks every rule of the form. Woolf wrote it as a playful love letter to her friend Vita Sackville-West, whose family home and ancestors fill its pages. It became her best-selling book during her life.

Orlando begins as a young Elizabethan nobleman and lives on for three hundred years. Partway through, in Constantinople, Orlando sleeps for days and wakes as a woman. The story sweeps through the Great Frost, Augustan coffeehouses, and Victorian damp to reach 1928. Woolf mocks biography, history, and gender itself with delight. Beneath the jokes sits a serious portrait of a writer's inner life.
lewis-man-who-knew-coolidge-1928:
Sinclair Lewis published The Man Who Knew Coolidge in 1928, a short comic novel built as a single endless monologue. Its speaker, Lowell Schmaltz, is a traveling salesman and proud clubman from Zenith, the same fictional city as Babbitt. Lewis called the book a pendant to Babbitt, its hero's booster cousin at full length.

Schmaltz buttonholes the reader with his great claim: he knew President Coolidge at college, slightly. Around that boast he pours out lodge talk, business creeds, Prohibition dodges, and opinions on everything in America. The comedy is in the voice itself, complacent, slangy, and utterly sure. Lewis catches a whole class talking in its sleep. The book is minor Lewis but perfect of its kind.
hurston-how-it-feels-to-be-colored-me-19:
How It Feels to Be Colored Me, published in 1928 in the magazine World Tomorrow, is Zora Neale Hurston's best-known essay. Hurston recalls growing up in Eatonville, Florida, where she first felt simply herself. She says she became colored when she moved to Jacksonville at age thirteen and felt set apart.

Rather than plead or boast, Hurston meets race with wit and self-assurance. She refuses pity and declares she does not feel tragically colored. Everyday images carry her points: colored bags of odds and ends, the feel of music, the shock of being watched. The essay became the most quoted personal statement of the Harlem Renaissance.
pillow-book-waley-1928:
Arthur Waley translated The Pillow-Book of Sei Shonagon into English in 1928, the first version to bring it to Western readers. Sei Shonagon, a lady of the Heian court around the year 1000, served the Empress Teishi in Kyoto. Her book is a classic of zuihitsu, the flowing miscellany of lists, scenes, and sharp opinions.

She lists things that quicken the heart, things that are hateful, and sparrows, clouds, and court gossip between. Her wit is quick and her eye for dress, weather, and folly is unmatched. Waley selected and arranged the material with a poet's tact. The Pillow-Book now stands beside The Tale of Genji as Heian Japan's gift to world letters.
thompson-epic-of-gilgamish-1928:
R. Campbell Thompson published The Epic of Gilgamish at Oxford's Clarendon Press in 1928. He spells the hero Gilgamish throughout, following his reading of the tablets. Thompson, a British Museum Assyriologist, made his verse translation from a fresh collation of the cuneiform tablets in London.

Gilgamesh, king of Uruk, loses his friend Enkidu and journeys past death's waters seeking eternal life. He returns with a story, a plant lost to a snake, and hard wisdom about fame. Thompson renders the epic in English hexameters meant to echo its stride. His version was the standard interwar English Gilgamesh. Readers met in it the oldest epic hero whose tale survives.
bailey-greek-atomists-epicurus-1928:
Cyril Bailey's 1928 study traces one bold idea across six centuries: that all things are made of tiny solid atoms moving in empty space. Leucippus and Democritus first framed the theory in the fifth century BCE. Bailey follows it through Epicurus and ends with the Roman poet Lucretius.

He sets out how the early atomists explained sight, soul, and the birth of worlds without calling on gods. Then he shows how Epicurus softened the system with the swerve of atoms and a calm way of life. Bailey weighs the scant sources with care. His book became the landmark English account of ancient atomism and its long afterlife.
bacon-opus-majus-burke-1928:
Roger Bacon, a Franciscan friar at Oxford, sent his Opus Majus to the pope in 1267 as a plan to renew all learning. Robert Belle Burke gave the whole work its first complete English form in 1928, in two volumes. Bacon wrote with a bold claim: true knowledge comes from experience, tested and seen.

Seven parts treat the causes of error, theology and philosophy, the study of tongues, mathematics, the science of sight, and experimental science, ending with moral philosophy. Bacon describes lenses, flying craft, and engines his age had never built. His plea for experiment reads like a charter for modern science. Burke's version lets English readers follow the whole great design.
procopius-wars-gothic-3-dewing-1928:
The History of the Wars of Procopius ends with books seven and eight, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1928. Totila's Goths still hold Italy, and Justinian sends the eunuch general Narses with a great army to finish the war. Procopius brings his vast work to its close.

Narses crushes Totila at Taginae and ends the Gothic kingdom at Mons Lactarius. The last book sweeps wider, to Persia, the Danube, and the Slavs pressing the frontier. Italy lies saved and ruined at once, its cities emptied by twenty years of war. Procopius is the chief witness of the whole reconquest. His final books ask what the victory was worth.
anna-comnena-alexiad-dawes-1928:
Anna Comnena, daughter of the emperor Alexius I, wrote the Alexiad in her widowhood to tell her father's reign, from 1081 to 1118. Elizabeth Dawes translated the Greek into English in 1928. The work is the first great history known to be written by a woman. Anna wrote as a princess, a scholar, and a partisan.

Alexius fights Normans, Turks, and rebels, rebuilds an empire in ruins, and then meets the armies of the First Crusade. Anna eyes the western knights with awe and contempt at once. Her portraits of her father and of Bohemond still glow. The Alexiad is the key Byzantine source for the crusade and a family monument. Her learning shows on every page.
smith-rabia-the-mystic-1928:
Margaret Smith wrote the first Western study of Rabi'a al-Adawiyya, the slave girl of Basra who became the first great woman saint of Islam. Her book appeared from Cambridge in 1928. Rabi'a died in 801, famed for a love of God that asked no heaven and feared no hell.

Smith gathers the tales and sayings of Rabi'a from the Arabic sources and sets her among her fellow saints. She treats the women of early Islam and the growth of Sufi teaching on divine love. Rabi'a's lamp, her donkey, and her blunt prayers come alive in the telling. The book founded the study of women in Sufism in the West.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-2-:
The second volume of Edward G. Browne's Literary History of Persia, issued in 1928, runs from Firdawsi to Sa'di. These are the great centuries of Persian poetry, when the ghazal and the Sufi mathnawi came to flower. Browne surveys the age with extracts in his own English renderings throughout.

Sanai, Attar, and Rumi rise in these pages, and Omar Khayyam argues his way through the quatrains. Sa'di of Shiraz, the master of the Gulistan, closes the volume. Browne's love of Persia and his wide reading in its manuscripts give the survey its warmth. The book is the standard context for all Persian Sufi literature in English.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-4-:
The fourth volume of Edward G. Browne's Literary History of Persia, from 1928, covers modern times, from 1500 to 1924, and completes the set. Browne knew this Persia at first hand: he had lived there, and he backed its constitutional revolution with pen and purse. His survey runs from the Safavid court to the newspapers of his own day.

Shi'a court poetry, the decline of verse under the Qajars, and the new prose of reformers and satirists fill the chapters. Browne prints the voices of the constitutional age in his own translations. The set of four volumes remains the fullest English history of Persian letters. It ends as both scholarship and a love letter to a nation.
drake-world-encompassed-1628:
The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake, printed in 1628, tells of the second voyage ever made around the whole earth. Drake sailed from England in 1577 and came home in 1580, having raided Spain's Pacific coast and crossed oceans no Englishman had crossed. His nephew gathered the account from the journals of the voyage, decades after the return.

The narrative follows the fleet through storms, straits, and rich prizes, down to one ship and a hard homecoming. It was the first full English telling of the feat, issued long after Drake's death. The delay kept its details scarce goods among readers of travel. The book still carries the pride of a small nation tasting global reach.
hutcheson-essay-passions-illustrations-1:
Hutcheson's Essay on the Nature and Conduct of the Passions and Affections, from 1728, is the first edition of his psychology of feeling. Its second half, the Illustrations on the Moral Sense, defends his central idea against two critics, Gilbert Burnet and John Balguy. Francis Hutcheson taught at Glasgow, where he shaped a generation of Scottish thinkers.

The essay sorts our passions and affections: calm desires, violent storms, and the steady pull of benevolence. Hutcheson asks how reason should govern feeling without killing it. The Illustrations then argue that our approval of virtue comes from a moral sense planted in our nature. The book completes the system begun in his Inquiry of 1725.
schleiermacher-christian-faith-1928:
The Christian Faith, in the translation by H R Mackintosh and J S Stewart of 1928, is Friedrich Schleiermacher's Der christliche Glaube of 1821 to 1822. The English version is complete, and it carries the magnum opus of liberal Protestant theology. Schleiermacher spent a life preaching and teaching at Berlin, and this book gathers his whole system of doctrine.

His key phrase is the feeling of absolute dependence, the heart's sense of resting wholly on God. Every doctrine, from creation to the church to last things, is traced to that feeling in the believer's life. Critics call the system vast, subtle, and hard to storm. It still anchors the study of modern theology.
spr-proceedings-vol36-1926-1928:
Volume thirty six gathers parts ninety seven through one hundred three, spanning 1926 to 1928. Seven parts in one binding close the run of Proceedings held here. The Society for Psychical Research had published since 1882, testing wonders by committee rule. Telepathy, apparitions, and trance mediumship fill these last parts as they filled the first.

Sittings, surveys, and spontaneous cases stand reported with the old care. The archive these volumes build is the primary record of the evidential debate to 1930. No verdict ends it; the files simply stand open. Volume thirty six completes the set on this shelf. Readers can now cross the whole span in order.
mead-coming-of-age-in-samoa-1928:
Margaret Mead went to Samoa as a young researcher and returned with Coming of Age in Samoa, published in 1928. Her study follows Samoan girls through adolescence, asking whether teenage turmoil is nature or culture. Custom, rank, and the religious regulation of youth shape the lives she watched on the island of Ta'u.

Mead's answer, that Samoan teens grew up with little of America's storm, made the book famous worldwide. It carried anthropology to a vast public and set off arguments that ran for decades. Few scholarly books have changed so many readers' picture of their own society.
jochelson-peoples-of-asiatic-russia-1928:
Waldemar Jochelson spent years in Siberia with the Jesup North Pacific Expedition, studying the native peoples of the far northeast. His 1928 survey gathers that work into one broad account of the peoples of Asiatic Russia, from the Yukaghir and Koryak to the Tungus groups.

Jochelson describes how each people lived: their hunting, fishing, homes, dress, and family life across a harsh land. He gives much space to shamanism, the spirit world, and the rites used against illness and bad luck. Because he recorded much of this before Soviet rule transformed the region, his survey preserves ways of life that soon vanished.
eliot-for-lancelot-andrewes-1928:
Eliot named this 1928 essay collection for Lancelot Andrewes, the Jacobean bishop and preacher whose sermons he admired. The title signals the book's subject: the meeting of style and belief in prose and poetry.

The essays cover Andrewes, Machiavelli, and the problem of writing religious prose in a doubting age. In the preface Eliot famously declared himself a classicist in literature, a royalist in politics, and an Anglo-Catholic in religion. That sentence shocked readers and fixed his public image for years. The book marks his turn from restless experiment toward order, tradition, and faith. It gathers the criticism of his conversion years.
ford-last-post-1928:
Last Post, published in 1928, closes Parade's End on a single long country day after the war. The armistice is past, Tietjens's brother Mark lies dying and silent, and the family's great house passes out of their hands for good.

Tietjens now lives with Valentine Wannop, selling antiques, while Sylvia's last maneuvers fail to reclaim him. Ford views the aftermath largely through other minds, letting the old order's end arrive quietly. Some readers find the volume a falling-off; others prize its elegy. Either way, it completes modernism's broadest portrait of England at war and in uneasy peace.
russell-sceptical-essays-1928:
Sceptical Essays, published in 1928, collects Russell's shorter pieces applying rational doubt to religion, morals, politics, and everyday belief. His prescription is in the first essay: when the experts disagree, the non-expert does well to doubt.

Essay by essay he examines free thought, the dangers of propaganda, and the harm done by good intentions armed with power. Russell writes as a public teacher, witty and exact, refusing every comfortable fog. The targets change with the years, but the method never dates. These essays show the most famous skeptic of the century at his most readable and most humane.
benda-treason-intellectuals-1928:
The Treason of the Intellectuals, published in French in 1927, appeared in English in 1928 in Richard Aldington's translation. It is Julien Benda's famous indictment of his fellow thinkers. Its charge: the clerks, whose calling was truth, had betrayed it for political passion.

Benda attacks writers who put nation, race, or class above universal values of justice and reason. He names the new cult of the particular as the age's spiritual crime. The book became a byword, quoted in every later quarrel over intellectuals and power. Its austerity still stings, and its question has never gone away.
plos-pone-0003428:
Joep P. M. Derikx and co-authors studied gut injury and repair in people in this 2008 paper. When blood flow to the intestine stops and returns, the lining gets hurt. This harm, called ischemia-reperfusion injury, follows events like aortic surgery. Animal studies had told only part of the story.

In human patients, the injured lining cells were shed quickly. Fresh lining then grew back over the gut surface fast. That rapid repair reversed much of the early damage. The finding gives surgeons a clearer picture of how the human gut heals.
plos-pone-0003528:
Pascal F. Egea, Johanna Napetschnig, and Peter Walter solved protein structures in this 2008 paper. The signal recognition particle grabs new proteins bound for membranes or export. It acts as those proteins emerge from the ribosome. Two proteins, SRP54 and SRP19, organize its RNA core.

The team worked with versions from Pyrococcus furiosus, a heat-loving microbe. Atomic structures show how the two proteins frame the core. The particle's design is conserved across all life. Such pictures reveal how the universal shipping machine is assembled. Heat-loving microbes give sturdy proteins that are easier to crystallize and read.
plos-pone-0003628:
Miriam Dyck, Maren Winbeck, Susanne Leiberg, and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It tests whether people read emotions in computer-made faces as well as in real ones. Virtual faces are now realistic enough to use as test material in emotion research.

Volunteers judged the feelings shown by natural faces and by virtual faces. The authors compared how well each type of face was read. The results show where digital faces work as stand-ins for real ones and where they fall short. That guidance matters for labs that use avatars in studies and therapy.
plos-pone-0003728:
Anahi Molla-Herman, Cedric Boularan, Rania Ghossoub, and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Most cells carry a primary cilium, a thin sensing bristle built from the centrosome when the cell rests. It samples the cell's surroundings and helps run key processes.

The team tracked beta-arrestin2, a well-known signaling protein, to the centrosome and primary cilium. There it plays a part in controlling how cells proliferate. The placement links a classic signaling player to the organelle that senses the world outside the cell. That role puts the cilium at the heart of cell growth control.
plos-pone-0003828:
Hong Lu, Prabhu Patil, Marie-Anne Van Sluys, and colleagues published this plant bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Xanthomonas is a large genus of bacteria that cause disease on more than 392 plant species. Each strain shows marked loyalty to certain hosts and tissues. What decides that specificity was unknown.

The team studied how gene clusters tied to pathogenesis were acquired and evolved in these bacteria. They searched for candidate determinants of tissue specificity among the clusters. The work maps how plant pathogens assemble their weapon kits as they adapt to chosen hosts.
plos-pone-0003928:
Courtney B. Field, Kevin Johnston, Joseph S. Gati, and co-authors mapped a primate brain hub's connections in 2008. Brain wiring was usually traced by injecting chemicals and viewing tissue later. Those methods cannot be used while an animal is alive and scanned. The team wanted a live method for the superior colliculus.

They paired tiny electric stimulation of the hub with whole-brain fMRI scans. The scans showed which areas responded when the hub was zapped. That traced its connections without any chemical tracers. The method opens live wiring maps for other deep brain areas too.
plos-pone-0004028:
Tawee Chotpitayasunondh, Usa Thisyakorn, Chitsanu Pancharoen, and co-authors trialed a bird flu vaccine in children in 2008. H5N1 influenza has caused outbreaks in birds across several continents. Human infections, often in children, have been severe and deadly. Human-to-human spread stayed limited, but the threat remained.

Their PLOS ONE article tested two forms of an inactivated H5N1 vaccine. They measured safety plus antibody and cell-mediated immune responses. Children are a priority group for pandemic vaccine planning. Data in children cannot simply be assumed from adult trials. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004128:
Luca Beltrame and colleagues published this methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microarrays measure the activity of thousands of genes at once, and labs have built up huge public stores of such data. Finding which stored experiments resemble each other has become a major challenge for researchers.

Instead of comparing single genes, the authors propose pathway signatures, patterns drawn from defined groups of genes that work together. They use these signatures as the basis for judging how similar two microarray experiments are. The approach gives scientists a practical way to search public data and spot links between studies done for different reasons.
plos-pone-0004228:
Juanita Bezuidenhout and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Granulomas, balls of immune cells that wall off stubborn germs, are an essential defence against persistent infection. They can also damage the tissue they defend. The team asked whether HIV co-infection changes that balance in pleural tuberculosis, infection of the lung's lining.

They compared the look and cytokine profile of granulomas in patients with early HIV infection. They report increased expression of TNF-alpha and more necrosis, dead tissue, in those granulomas. The finding shows how HIV can make a defence structure more destructive.
plos-pone-0004328:
Richard Hunter and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kainate receptors are a class of glutamate receptors that modulate glutamate release and synaptic plasticity in the hippocampal formation, a memory centre. Earlier work had tied corticosteroids, the stress hormones, to the control of these receptors, and recent clinical work pointed the same way.

The team measured how stress and corticosteroids change the levels of kainate receptor subunit messenger RNA in the rat hippocampus. Which subunits rise or fall shapes how the memory centre behaves under stress. The study connects the hormone surge of a bad day to the wiring of memory.
plos-pone-0004428: In 2009, Zimmermann, Kring, and Berentzen found a fat gene's darker side. An FTO gene variant raised mortality independent of fatness in Danish cohorts. The risk allele killed beyond obesity. The finding reframes the famous fat gene. The cohorts were large.
plos-pone-0004528: In 2009, Nasser, Kaplan, and Nevo profiled a burrowing oddball's blood fats. Lipid profiles of the blind subterranean mole rat Spalax were charted. The burrower's serum adapted to low-oxygen life. The finding maps hypoxia adaptation tricks. The rat lives fully underground.
plos-pone-0004628: In 2009, Wang, Wu, and Qin found a mineral guarding guts against a nasty germ. Low selenium raised gut harm from Cryptosporidium. The mineral-poor hosts suffered more badly. The finding links food and defense research. The test germ was tiny C parvum.
plos-pone-0004728: In 2009, a team found a tumor enzyme fueling drug resistance anew here. MMP7's chat with the FAS/FASL system during resistance was studied. The enzyme blunted the drug badly. The study informs chemo design. The drug resistance is acquired.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-28:
War returns in full force in Volume 28, from 1898. Thwaites covers the Hurons and Iroquois across 1646 and 1647, as peace fails. The annual report turns into a chronicle of slow disaster for Huronia.

Raids burn towns, scatter families, and close the river routes again. Priests write on, steady as ever, while their world crumbles. They bury the dead, guard the fleeing, and keep the chapels open. Each letter home carries grief, grit, and unshaken purpose at once. The volume shows a mission in its last years, still at work each day. Its writers refuse despair even as towns fall.
kellogg-briand-pact-1928:
In 1928, leading nations signed a short pact in Paris renouncing war as a tool of national policy. It took its name from its two sponsors, American Secretary of State Frank Kellogg and French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand. Germany, Japan, and the Soviet Union were among the early signers, and sixty-two nations joined in time.

The signers promised to settle all disputes by peaceful means and never to seek their aims through war. The pact carried no army and no penalties, and within a decade several signers were at war. Still, it wrote into law the idea that aggressive war is a crime, a principle later used at the Nuremberg trials.
coke-institutes-part1-1628:
Edward Coke published the First Part of the Institutes in 1628, built as a commentary on Littleton's old book on land tenures. Lawyers call it Coke upon Littleton, and it became the most famous law book in English history. Coke, once chief justice and later a leader of Parliament against the crown, poured a lifetime of learning into its notes.

Page by page, the commentary turns a short medieval text into a full course in property law. Coke explains estates, inheritances, and the duties of lords and tenants, citing cases old and new. For two centuries, law students learned their profession from this book, and its authority in court was nearly unmatched. It stands as the oracle of the common law in its classical age.
senior-two-lectures-population-1828:
Senior's Two Lectures on Population, delivered at Oxford in 1828, give his answer to Malthus on the great question of the age. Malthus had taught that population grows faster than food, so misery must check the numbers. Senior grants the race between mouths and loaves but disputes the finish.

He adds the check Malthus slighted: prudence. As people grow more decent in their wants, Senior argues, they delay marriage and limit families to protect their standard of life. The desire for improvement can thus outrun the pressure of numbers. The lectures soften the gloomy science with common sense and were praised for their humanity. They include his exchange with Malthus himself, who answered in letters printed with the lectures. The old classical school appears here at its most humane.
petition-of-right-1628:
Parliament sent the Petition of Right to King Charles I in 1628, at a time of sharp conflict over royal power. Led by figures such as Edward Coke, members listed old rights they said the king had broken. They asked him to accept clear limits, not to grant new favors.

The petition protests taxes raised without consent, arrests without a stated cause, and soldiers lodged in private homes. It also objects to martial law used against civilians in peacetime. Charles agreed to it, then kept quarreling with Parliament anyway. Later generations treated the petition as a founding text of English liberty.
cia-0000009828:
A deleted source's account of hearing that American pilots were still being held is preserved in a January 1966 item. The name is blacked out, as sources' names usually were on release. Hearsay sits low in the evidence order, and the heading keeps it plainly labeled.

Secondhand claims still entered the files because a man's fate might ride on them. Analysts marked the chain of telling: who heard, from whom, and where. Later reports could raise or sink such an account. This file shows the bottom layer of the prisoner record, rumor kept because silence risked more.
cia-0000012428:
Parts three and four of the Penkovsky operation, taped on October 22, 1966, form an audio retrospective of the case. Four years after the colonel's arrest, the service recorded its own spoken history of the operation. The tapes narrate the case whole: approach, debriefings, product, and loss, told aloud by men looking back on the defining episode of their careers.

The retrospective's calm narration belies the stakes the operation once carried. Its value is memory fixed before the witnesses scattered. For readers, the record points to the great case remembered in voices, not only in files.
cia-0000013228:
The rulebook of the southern camps is set out in a CIA paper from July 1970. It covers Viet Cong policies and procedures for American prisoners in a military region. Read closely, the rules show a machine built to hold men. Intake, questioning, movement, punishment, and release all appear as steps. Each is reduced to dry procedure in the enemy's own administrative language, as if captivity were office work.

The files keep the manual because manuals tell the truth about systems. This one governed real cages and real guards in the jungle. For readers, the paper is the camp system written out like routine, which is its horror.
cia-0000015428: Sara B. Hunt met an Air Force request in July 1966 to declassify a CIA paper on UFOs, a record filed June 3, 1966. The paper at issue was the February 1953 report of the Scientific Panel on Unidentified Flying Objects. A CBS program had stirred press interest in the agency's role. The memo shows secrecy itself becoming the story officials had to manage.
cia-0000022328: The altitude of Powers' U-2, with his father mentioned in documents, fills a CIA record dated in 1960. How high the plane flew mattered, since America had claimed such flights stayed out of reach. His father spoke out during the trial weeks in Moscow. The pairing joins a hard fact of the flight to the family's public pain that summer.

Each numbered case was one man's file in the long search for the missing.
cia-0000022828: A briefing on the status of Colonel Patrick M. Fallon, of the Air Force, missing in Laos, fills a CIA record dated in 1972. The person briefed had his name deleted before release. Fallon's case was one of many Laos losses that stayed unresolved for years. A status briefing meant his file was still active, still read, and still open.

cia-0000037028:
Lieutenant James K. Patterson is the subject of photo comparison results in a CIA record dated January 2, 1971. The work draws on the Christmas film of 1969, which showed prisoners held in North Vietnam. Patterson was missing, and the film offered a chance to learn his fate at last.

Analysts studied the film's faces and set them against Patterson's known photographs. Their findings gave his case a firm entry in the record, one way or the other. The file belongs to the same Christmas 1969 effort that produced many numbered results across the MIA and POW caseload that winter.
cia-0000044428:
The opposition said the government was responsible for the priest killings, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Opposition parties rarely spoke so bluntly without risk in that war. Their charge named the state itself, not a rogue unit.

Inside, the opposition's accusation is preserved at full strength. To call a government responsible is to deny it good faith entirely. Such words raised the cost of every compromise that followed. The file keeps the charge as it was made, a measure of how far trust between El Salvador's government and its critics had fallen that autumn.
cia-0000045028:
A Japanese source said American prisoners were seen in Vietnam in 1988, in a CIA record dated May 3, 1989. The claim reached the files fifteen years after the war's end. Reports from third-country witnesses had a long history in this search.

Inside, the sighting claim is recorded with its source described. A witness from outside the war could seem free of old loyalties. That freedom made such reports hard to file away and forget. The record preserves one late claim from 1989, in the years when the live-prisoner question still drew believers, skeptics, and official patience in equal measure.
cia-0000045228:
An agreement was virtually reached on the Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated September 4, 1985. Virtually reached is a phrase that carries its own warning. Near deals in kidnapping cases collapse as often as they close.

Inside, the near settlement of the case is recorded as reported. Terms were close enough to be described as an agreement in waiting. What remained between the sides was small in words and large in risk. The file preserves that hopeful and fragile moment, one of several turns in which the young woman's freedom seemed close enough to touch.
cia-0000045928: Officials presented what they called concrete proof that an American pilot had died, and a CIA item dated June 5, 1991, carries the claim. For families of the missing, such proof could end years of waiting and doubt. The item belongs to the hard accounting of 1991, when each case was argued over piece by piece.
cia-0000049228: Stanley Moskowitz, the CIA's director of congressional affairs, wrote to Senator Paul Simon in 1992, and the letter survives in this item. Such letters kept the oversight machinery oiled: information promised, questions answered, tempers managed. This one sits among the records of the Jesuit case years, when Congress watched the agency closely.
cia-0000098728: Economic Cooperation with U.S. Desired is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098728, dated September 3, 1989. The title does not say whose desire it records.
